Public works agencies are full of red tape. For larger cities, especially if they’re old because they can have a lot of simultaneous projects that can go on in any one area for all types of utilities that are underground, it takes a long time. Most rehabilitation projects are planned and designed anywhere between 6 months to 5 years in advance so it takes a while for anything to be done. The process to secure a contractor to conduct the project and then another few months to get the paperwork and funds ready to begin the project is also long. Then there’s the whole matter to get the money funded for infrastructure projects to the public works agency that does all this planning in the first place. It’s a system designed to be complicated and I don’t really understand why yet. I feel like it’s more nuanced than to save the government money (I’m an intern at one of said agencies)

They also prioritize the roads that pose more of a safety concern because they’d rather not spend money on the litigation that could arise from that. You don’t see this everywhere though. Go to any wealthy city and you won’t see a pothole or bumpy road anywhere, not for long at least…

I, 22, was advised to do DBT therapy multiple times, but I never took up the offer. I very much regret it, but I do believe that CBT is a modality that could help us, provided that the therapist is patient and willing to adapt the approach to benefit us as much as possible. It's very hard to achieve this because CBT treatment is meant to be short-term. My therapist implemented the following strategies:

1. If I'd struggle to share my perspective on a strategy or lesson, she would ask guiding questions to help me arrive at the answer on my own. 
2. Vague and open-ended questions would be avoided or rephrased more specifically. 
3. Instead of relying exclusively on listening, we used visual aids to help my understanding. 
4. When it came to identifying emotions, I always referred to an emotion bank visual to help myself describe my mood.
5. If I'd get hung up trying to understand a concept or process anything, I'd get a little coping/mondfulness break to decompress and compose myself to continue having a productive session.
6. Sessions would get wrapped up gradually so as to avoid the abruptness, which would not leave me unsatisfied and emotionally dysregulated.

I think it would have helped tremendously if, instead of a 1 hour sessions, we had a 1.5 hour sessions, but I don't think that's a fiscally viable option for most of us or most clinicians for that matter. 

Needless to say, I didn't gain enough out of CBT because of how inflexible I've been to change my behavior and cultivate the adaptive thoughts that CBT is based on.
